[The text explains] "arising," saying: he understands as it really is the escape from that. Thus, as to the sensation connected with the jhanas of the one who has that, it occurs accordingly. Regarding the states connected with the four jhanas, and whatever states are such, by means of understanding them the sensation connected with the four jhanas is seen. Thus, by the attainment of the (meditator's own) disposition, there are four attainments: the three liberations and the obtainable internal liberation. "Jhana" means the four jhanas. "Liberation" means the internal and the three liberations and the obtainable liberations. Concentration: there are four kinds of concentration — concentration of zeal, concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of view. "Attainments" means the four dispositional attainments. Thus, regarding these jhanas, it is said there is "attainment of liberation." In such a case, the defilement of a person of lustful temperament is thus; of a person of hateful temperament, of a person of deluded temperament — such is the sensation. Thus this knowledge of his, as it really is, uncommon to all beings — this is called the first power of the Tathagata.

Herein the Tathagata understands thus: mundane states and supramundane states, in the sphere of development and manifestation — regarding "faculties" they take hold, having taken the ground of predominance; regarding "powers" they take hold, having taken mind and mental faculty; regarding "energy" they take hold, having taken the element of initiative. Thus his knowledge of such a kind is: "these persons are endowed with these qualities." He gave a Dhamma-talk accordingly and otherwise, regarding the disposition and inclination, endowed with resolve. This is called the knowledge of the faculties, powers, and energy of other beings, of other persons — the seventh power of the Tathagata.

Herein, too, the Tathagata understands the destiny with respect to the fetters, in the worlds and elsewhere, among the bases, of the trainees' view and power. By the recollection of past lives, in the past round of existence, as it was then, and the passing away and rearising by the divine eye — thus these two powers exist from the divine eye. Not previously, this one of divine sort goes in... that is, as to the present, the sphere of mindfulness; thus, of himself and of others, the knowledge of past lives, manifold and of various kinds, giving the ability to see the passing away and rearising. These are the two powers of the Tathagata: the eighth, recollection of past lives; the ninth, the divine eye.

Furthermore, the Tathagata understands the sensation connected with the states of noble persons, in regard to penetration: "This person, by this path, by this practice, from the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having attained it, dwells in it." Thus, of himself, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints — by this, having taken hold of the four bases, up to not returning for arahantship — is for the trainees who have not yet reached arahantship. Herein, liberation of mind that is free from the taints — the sense-desire taint and the taint of becoming; liberation by wisdom that is free from the taints — the taint of views and the taint of ignorance. The knowledge, as it really is, of these liberations of view — this is called the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

This is the tenth power of the Tathagata.

54                                                           Petakopadesa - Sasana Pradhana

Therein, what word points to personality-view? It says: "That life, that
body" - referring to those who are confused, to those who are arisen accidentally, and
those who act in all states, and those who experience in all states, leading to the final
feeling. [?] Three terms belong to personality-view
and are eternal. "In all beings, life; in all beings, body" means inaction
in regard to suffering: it falls without cause, and (asserts) in states of non-cessation
the equality of all actions.1

Therein, "This alone is true, all else is false" - this is proclaimed by
wandering ascetics who confuse themselves in the cycle of existence. Just as personality-view
has four bases, so too, among the various bonds, twenty bases2
belong eternally to personality-view.
Wanderers of various kinds and eternalists3 cling to rules and vows, holding them supreme,
thinking "by this means we shall purify ourselves," and thus roam from state to state among beings.
This is the supremacy of attachment to rules and vows.

Therein, one by personality-view regards form as self: "that is
life, that is body." He does, he doubts, he does not resolve, he does not find confidence,
regarding the past, the future, the past-and-future - and so on - this is
the defilement of the cold (confusion) arising from such dispositions.

Therein, through right understanding he abandons all that should be thoroughly rejected;
through the faculty of wisdom he sees rise and fall; through the faculty of concentration
he unifies the mind; through the faculty of energy
he strives. By these five faculties, one following the Dhamma, intent on
unshakable confidence, develops unbroken concentration. By means of well-purified faculties,
one following the Dhamma, free from falling away, develops unbroken concentration. He
understands as it really is: "This is suffering." (The truths) - this is a teaching bound up with vision.
By the abandonment through vision of the three fetters pertaining to the lower (bonds) belonging to
that person — these three fetters are to be abandoned through vision5 — entirely all
are destroyed, both kinds being included. [?]

Therein, the three that are to be abandoned by cultivation [of the path], being examined above,
lead to Nibbāna. Therein, when covetousness and ill-will are attenuated in them,
the state becomes limited,6 reaching a boundary, and that state is inevitable. For him,
covetousness and ill-will are, in both respects, entirely destroyed. Thus
that state is unshakeable. He is said to be one in whom conceit "I am" is extinguished. Even for the trainee,
there remain subtle defilements: attachment to form-existence, attachment to formless-existence, ignorance,
restlessness, and the conceit "I am."7 Through the strength of the path, when the conceit "I am" is overturned,
even then the abandonment of the conceit "I am" is to be attained.8 Regarding defilements in general and those remaining,
this matter of vision, pertaining to the many factors and to the practice of the noble ones,9
and to those who have gone beyond — this is a teaching bound up with cultivation, further than that.10 Those possessing various knowledges—

The Fifth Section (Pañcadama Bhūmi)

What, then, are the divisions of the "exposition" (hāra)? That which proceeds through the sixteen modes of letters/syllables—

1. The manner of the exposition at its beginning: On that point there is this verse:

Whether wholesome or unwholesome,
whether "all" or "in part"—
what is said and heard,
is the examination of the manner of exposition.

As in "the noble truths¹" as the analysis: the four truths, whether common or uncommon, or in whichever eighteen terms concerning suffering: seven terms are summed up as suffering due to bodily pain, mental pain, the suffering of disagreeable contact, and the suffering of separation from the agreeable, and by three determinate states² there, the three characteristics of the determinate are set forth as suffering: arising is the characteristic of the determinate; the suffering of formations is suffering, and specially, the determinate³ characteristic; the suffering of change is suffering, and⁴ non-independence⁵ is the characteristic of the determinate; the suffering of suffering⁷ is suffering,⁸ — these three characteristics of the determinate, in the three planes of feeling, there is also the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant: arising is the characteristic of the determinate, the suffering of formations and suffering, specially⁹ the characteristic of the determinate, pleasant feeling¹⁰ and the suffering of change and suffering,¹⁰ non-independence is the characteristic of the determinate, painful feeling, the suffering of suffering, and suffering — thus in these¹¹ nine terms, in the first seven terms, in the sixteen terms, suffering is to be sought; and the characteristic of the eleven forms of suffering is set out in the exposition. The characteristic of manifestation is "birth," and that which is the characteristic of the occurrence of manifestation — thus, in detail, fifteen terms are to be made.

Thus, in common and uncommon [terms], in the seven and in the ten terms, in the recollection of mindfulness¹¹, in the foundation of the teaching¹² in the eighteen modes, and in the ten modes of doctrine designation, and in the sixteen modes of the exposition (hāra), and in the twenty-one modes of the examination of conditions (paccaya) — this was taught. And it was taught as it truly is. This is the manner of exposition.

Petakopadesa, Seventh Bundle

And what is the perfection of body [conduct]: the perfection, loving-kindness [is explained by] "beings attached to sensual pleasures, beings bound by sensual pleasures" — in whichever discourse, by the method of teaching, all things are shown by way of suffering and its arising. By the method of intention. Those who, among the states connected with the fetters, do not see the fault, [thinking] "we shall cross over" — this is not possible. [Thinking] "we shall not cross over" is wrong; this [teaching] exists as the bound ones' very wish.

Now, what is the proximate cause of this: for beings attached to sensual pleasures — the five strands of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause of craving for sensual pleasure; [this is explained] in terms of seeing the fault in the fetters. Ignorance is the proximate cause; without the destruction of the fetters, bound beings create for themselves a broad, extensive accumulation [of suffering] — this is the proximate cause of what arises further.

For beings attached to sensual pleasures: sensual pleasures are of two kinds, pleasures of basis (objects) and pleasures of defilement. Among these, defilement-pleasure is craving for sensual pleasure; bound by craving for sensual pleasure, beings exist [bound also] by craving for form and craving for existence — by way of characteristic. Regarding seeing the fault in the fetters: of the fetter, whatever is desire-and-lust, what is its proximate cause? Two faculties, namely pleasant feeling — the faculty of bodily pleasure and the faculty of mental joy. Thus, when pleasant feeling is grasped, that feeling too is thereby grasped. When the aggregate of feeling is grasped, all the five aggregates are grasped. Form, perception, and tangible objects are grasped; when the pleasures of sense-objects are grasped, all the external internal sense bases also become grasped. Among the internal and external sense bases, whatever being there is — this is called, by way of characteristic.

Among these, one who is not attached to coarse defilements, [but is still] attached to all [other] defilements, is still free from passion only with regard to the subtler ones. Among these, the external fetter is called "mine"; the internal fetter is called "I am."

What is the Blessed One's intention here? Those who wish to cross over will dwell contemplating the danger in states connected with the fetters — this is the Blessed One's intention: beings attached to sensual pleasures, those among whom there are beings, by which there are beings, of which there are beings — this is the fourfold mode in the entire exposition of formations.

And what are the three distortions (vipallāsa) and their proximate causes: distortion of mind, distortion of view, and distortion of perception — these three distortions are the proximate cause of the three unwholesome roots. The three unwholesome roots are the proximate cause of inferior and superior kinds of action. As a fourth, with respect to clinging, two unwholesome roots appear as the proximate cause of inferior and superior kinds of action — just as, with respect to mother and father, and to one even more pure, a higher bhikkhu, [one who] grants safety. Among these, one who acts wrongly by body and speech — among these, whoever, having taken on ill-will toward those who protect and guard the noble ones, fails to protect them; whoever grants safety to the noble ones, having seen their safety, and yet acts wrongly toward them — such a one harbors ill-will, giving rise to a defiled action.

222
Petakopadesa — The Seventh Ground (Sattabhūmi)

Therein, one who views thus, "This I am," regards form as self; one regards equanimity and so forth, and the possessor of form as self, and in self the form, or form in self, or self in form — thus the view of equanimity, and so forth. One falls away from the view of a being, and falls away from the prior-end view. One does not regard "This I am." For such a one, the abandoning of all views comes about. In that threefold darkness — regarding the prior end and regarding the posterior end — by that very designation.

Whatever season, friend, among all who are free of passion, does not continue to view "I am" through this reverence, through this effort, through this method. This is the ground of vision and the fruit of stream-entry. For one practiced in noble effort, through the cycle of existence gone to non-being, of those who are 'not to be reborn' — whatever noble effort there is for not being reborn again, whether in the five faculties mild, medium, or strong, all conduces to the abandonment of rebirth. "I" — in view, in desire, in existence, in ignorance, and in the moment.

1. Therein, by the method of teaching there are four truths. By the five faculties and by the fruit of stream-entry, all these are the path and cessation. By the origin of personality-belief, all these are suffering and its origin — this is the method of teaching.

2. Therein, what is investigation? In one who does not regard "This I am," the fetters to be abandoned by vision are abandoned — this is investigation.

3. Therein, what is suitability? There are three kinds of persons: one who has grasped the aggregates by learning, one who has seen the aggregates through insight, and one who is to be guided. The one who has grasped by learning has sharp faculties; following that, the one who has seen through insight has faculties of medium strength; following that, the one with mild faculties is to be guided.

Therein, the one who has grasped the aggregates by learning, through sharpness of faculties, attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision, and becomes "one-seeded" (reborn only once more). This is the first type of stream-enterer. The one who has seen the aggregates through insight, with mild faculties, attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision, and becomes a "family-to-family" one (reborn in good families repeatedly). This is the second type of stream-enterer. Therein, the one who is to be guided attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision and becomes one who is reborn at most seven times. This is the third type of stream-enterer.

Therein, this is the suitability: with mild, medium, or strong faculties, one realizes the ground that is mild, medium, or strong, and through abandoning personality-belief, abandons all wrong views. This is suitability.

4. Therein, what is the proximate cause? Therein, personality-belief is the proximate cause for all wrong views; in personality (existence), name-and-form is the proximate cause; name-and-form is the proximate cause for personality-belief; the five material faculties are the proximate cause for materiality; the six sense bases are the proximate cause for volitional formations.

276                                                    The Petakopadesa — Explanation of the Method

"And he feels it" means: it shows the inclusion of purification. "And he lies latent" means: it shows the inclusion of the latent tendency. "And he feels it" means: it shows the abandonment of the gross defilements. "And he lies latent" means: it shows the abandonment of the subtle defilements. "And he feels it" means: the cause(?) and the plane. "And he discards it" means: the once-returner and the non-returner. "And he lies latent" means: the arahant. "And he feels it" shows the abandonment through the opposite of one accomplished in virtue. "And he discards it" shows the abandonment through the opposite of one accomplished in concentration. "And he lies latent" shows the abandonment through the opposite of one accomplished in wisdom. "And he feels it" shows the abandonment of formations pertaining to the lesser degree of perception. "And he lies latent" shows the abandonment of formations pertaining to the higher-trainee degree. "And he feels it" is the faculty associated with the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "And he discards it" is the faculty without sound. "And he lies latent" is the faculty in the state of non-restraint. "And he feels it" is the development of the soft faculty. "And he discards it" is the development of the middling faculty. "And he lies latent" is the development of the intense faculty. This is the way according to the discourse.

1. Herein, what is the teaching? Here in the discourse, the Four Truths are taught.

2–3. Whatever is felt and whatever is conceived — even that object establishes the mind, examines it, and applies itself. "And he feels it," "and he discards it" — even that object, through the latent tendency, dissolves and is examined and applied; he feels it and he discards it. Through the abandonment of the latent tendency, the dissolved state is sought out. It is applied as examination. This is called investigation according to the discourse.

4. Herein, what is the proximate cause? The purification of feeling is the proximate cause for the purification of feeling. The accumulation [of volitional formations] is the proximate cause for clinging. The purification of the latent tendencies is the proximate cause; for them, through the development leading to dispersal, there is the abandonment of attachment to becoming.

5. Herein, what is the characteristic? Whatever among the feelings is felt — that which is conceived, warmed, and dissolved — that dissolution occurs as a condition with respect to the object.

6. Herein, what is the fourfold intention? Here, in the discourse, the Blessed One's intention is: those who do not wish for the prior state, who do not feel it, and who discard it — this is the intention.

7. "To be entered into" means: whatever feeling, wisdom, latent tendency, dissolution, and abandonment there are — these are indeed truths.

8. "Investigation" means: that is the plane of investigation.

9. The restatement, however, is the complete rejection in practice.

[Page 304 - Petakopadesa, Chapter Seven]

By the glow of the minor marks [of the Buddha], the body shines like a sky full of risen stars, like a lotus pond in full bloom, like an assembly of a hundred suns gathered in sequence, [radiating] to thirty-six moons, thirty-six suns, thirty-six universal monarchs, thirty-six divine kingdoms, thirty-six great Brahmas — [this glory surpasses even] the glory of glory itself; it shines forth surrounded [by virtues]; the monks too, having renounced, content, secluded, uncontaminated, of aroused energy, speaking what should be spoken, bearing speech patiently, wise, blaming what is blameworthy, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration — and so on — (Commentary on the Sangiti Sutta.*)

Regarding "release" (nibbuti): is there release that is not of the non-learner (asekha)? (?)

10. "He feels joy" — for the giver, joy arises; for the one who rejoices [in another's giving], joy also arises. Whether through purity of mental disposition or through the act of rendering service, joy arises.

11. "Joy" — "for the giver joy arises" refers to the joy born of the abandonment of greed. "There is no enmity for one who is restrained" refers to the joy born of the abandonment of hatred. "The wise abandon evil" refers to the joy born of the abandonment of delusion.

12. "Otherwise" — joy arises for the giver in regard to the five faculties. For one who is restrained, there is no enmity; through restraint there is virtue — by this, restraint [of faculties arises]; wandering among the faculties — this is concentration. That which the wise abandon as evil — this is joy. The destruction of lust, hatred and delusion — that is release, [this is] liberation. Among the elements, it is the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhatu); among the sense-bases, it is the mind-base (manayatana).

13. "Investigates" — by whatever basis this discourse was taught, that is the basis to be understood.

14. "Resolve" — "giving" means joy arising from singleness of purpose. Generosity is relinquishment, teaching the Dhamma, and the giving of material things. Now, "giving" should be elaborated in detail — this is the variation. Thus for the giver, joy arises from the joy of single-purposedness. "Bondage" means the joy arising from the joy of non-distraction. "The destruction of lust, hatred and delusion — that is release" means the joy arising from the joy of strenuous energy.

15. "Equipment" — joy is the condition for giving, non-greed is the cause. Wise attention is the cause for restraint, and relinquishment is the condition. "The wise abandon evil" — right view is the condition, and freedom from the fever [of defilements] is the cause. "The destruction of lust, hatred and delusion — that is release" — external cessation and internal wise attention are both the Dhamma, the cause, and the condition.
